angle: An AI cleanup of 3 years of renewal data showed the renewal rate was worse than the board was told
post_first_line: Three years of renewal data. Nobody tracked it.
linkedin_post:
Three years of renewal data. Nobody tracked it.

The real renewal rate was worse than anyone had told the board.

Jeff Ignacio cleaned up a company's renewal database after the renewal process had been neglected for the last 3 years. Renewals were missing from 2023 to 2024.

The fix started with reconciling the records against Stripe data. Customers were still paying, so the payments showed what had actually happened.

From there, Jeff rebuilt the 2025 renewal base from those payments. Then came the closed-lost opportunities, so the team could run win rate analysis on renewals.

The result: the renewal rate was much worse than the company thought. It was also worse than the way the company had been pitching it to the board.

Not a happy outcome. But it's the moment the whole team realizes they're churning customers and need to plug the gap.

That's the ROI of clean data. You can't fix a leak you can't see.

When did you last audit your renewal data?

Slide 2: Renewals from 2023 to 2024 were missing entirely
Slide 3: Jeff Ignacio reconciled the records against Stripe payments
Slide 4: Paying customers revealed what actually happened
Slide 5: The 2025 renewal base was rebuilt from those payments
Slide 6: Closed-lost opps made renewal win rate analysis possible
Slide 7: The real renewal rate was worse than the board was told
Slide 8: You can't fix a leak you can't see

lesson.title: Clean renewal data shows the real churn problem
takeaways: Neglected renewal records can hide a renewal rate worse than leadership believes.
Payment data like Stripe is a reliable source of truth for reconciling who actually renewed.
Closed-lost tracking on renewals enables win rate analysis and shows where to plug the gap.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last 12 months of renewals and compare them to payment data. Flag every account where the CRM and payments disagree, then recalculate your renewal rate.

angle: The deals that 'close this month' and never do: how I stopped doing slipped-deal postmortems by hand
post_first_line: Every deal in commit says "closes this month."
linkedin_post:
Every deal in commit says "closes this month."

Some of them never do, and the way I used to deal with it was painful.

Anyone who's worked in RevOps knows this one. A rep calls a deal for the month, it sits in commit, and then it slips.

Every week we have a leadership call on forecast. I used to bring up the slipped deals myself and say, "this one actually slipped." Then I'd ask the rep why, which only gets you the rep's version of the story.

I wanted more context than that, so I changed how I run the analysis.

Now I have an agent go through all the calls in Attention. It does a postmortem on the deal and reads the SPICED notes. Then it tells me what was missing and what risk the rep had actually flagged.

It also checks my calendar for the next forecast leadership meeting. Before that meeting, the analysis lands in my Slack.

The summary covers the original close date and the root cause, plus where the rep missed something.

I used to walk into the forecast call with a list of slipped deals. Now I walk in with the reasons they slipped.

What's your process for slipped deals?
carousel: Slide 1: Deals in commit say "closes this month" and slip.
Slide 2: I used to bring slipped deals to forecast myself.
Slide 3: Asking the rep why only gets you one version.
Slide 4: Now an agent reviews every call on the deal.
Slide 5: It reads the SPICED notes and flags missing risk.
Slide 6: It checks my calendar for the next forecast meeting.
Slide 7: The postmortem lands in Slack before that meeting.
Slide 8: Original close date, root cause, and where the rep missed.

lesson.title: Automate the slipped-deal postmortem
takeaways: Asking the rep why a deal slipped only gives you their version. Call data gives you more context.
Time the analysis to your forecast meeting calendar so it arrives before the conversation.
A good postmortem covers the original close date, the root cause, and what the rep missed or flagged.
lesson.exercise: Pick one deal that slipped last month. Read its calls and notes, then write down the original close date, the root cause, and the risk the rep flagged. Use that as the template for automating the process.

caption: Stop hand-writing slipped deal postmortems

angle: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector so you don't have to. Here's the workaround
post_first_line: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector.
linkedin_post:
I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector.

I wouldn't recommend it.

I went deep down a rabbit hole trying to get an AI tool to read Salesforce data. The first thing you need is a connector with an MCP that can read a database, so the schema comes through. CData is one of those connectors.

I skipped past that and built my own anyway.

It meant a lot of building out Apex code and then deploying it. That's a lot of work for something a connector already does.

The better path is a middleware layer. Feed the data in through the middleware, and get your analysis in the meantime.

This was a real pain for me, and I'm sharing it so you can skip it.

Building it yourself feels like progress. It's mostly a detour.

What's a build you wish you'd bought instead?

Slide 3: That gives you the schema. CData is one example

lesson.title: Don't build the Salesforce MCP connector yourself
takeaways: You need a connector with an MCP that can read the database so the schema comes through.
Vibe coding your own Salesforce connector means building out and deploying Apex code, which is a lot of effort.

angle: Stop writing your own prompts: have Claude rewrite them using your CRM schema
linkedin_post:
Stop writing your own prompts.

I hand that job to Claude now, and the output is better than what I'd write.

I built a skill I call prompt enhancer. I drop in a rough prompt with a fair amount of context, and Claude reads my metadata and the Salesforce schema before rewriting it.

When I wrote "new business," Claude figured out I meant opportunity type new business. That alone excludes expansions, renewals, and all of that.

It also picked up forecast category names without me spelling them out.

Then it restructured the prompt into the original request, the intent, and the action that needs to happen.

We use SPICE internally, and I had notes on it in there. Claude went in and started finding the fields that apply to it. That part was mind-blowing.

The lesson: your CRM schema already holds the vocabulary your prompt is missing. Let the model read it instead of guessing at field names from memory.

What's one prompt you'd hand off first?
carousel: Slide 1: Stop writing your own prompts. Delegate it to Claude.
Slide 2: Build a skill that rewrites your rough prompt for you.
Slide 3: Claude reads your metadata and your Salesforce schema first.
Slide 4: "New business" becomes opportunity type new business. Renewals drop out.
Slide 5: It picks up forecast category names without being told.
Slide 6: Your prompt gets restructured: intent first, then the action.
Slide 7: It even found the fields that apply to our SPICE notes.
Slide 8: Your schema holds the vocabulary. Let the model read it.

lesson.title: Let Claude rewrite your prompts using your CRM schema
takeaways: Your rough prompt can be enhanced by a skill that reads your metadata and Salesforce schema.
Claude maps casual language like "new business" to exact fields like opportunity type, excluding expansions and renewals.
Structuring a prompt as original request, intent, and action makes the output clearer.
lesson.exercise: Write a rough prompt for a pipeline question you ask often. Give Claude your CRM schema and ask it to rewrite the prompt with exact field names, intent, and action. Compare the results of both versions.

caption: Let Claude write your prompts

angle: Don't use your smartest model for every step. Scoring 15,000 accounts of sales calls cost about $30
linkedin_post:
$30 to score 15,000 accounts.

The trick is knowing which step doesn't need your smartest model.

Jeff Ignacio's advice for the classification step: skip Claude Sonnet and use a lower-level model like Claude Haiku. If you're bold, something like DeepSeek on a Fireworks API works too. That dramatically brings down costs.

Jeff Ignacio's estimate was $30 to analyze the entire history of one sales team's calls across those 15,000 accounts.

Then the real questions open up:

What did the average MEDDIC score look like? Did each rep improve over time? Was there a difference between regrettable and non-regrettable attrition? Did improvement in MEDDIC correlate with improvement in performance?

Those are second, third, and fourth order questions. Most teams never get to them because they're still stuck building surface-level reporting.

Cheap models handle the repetitive step. That frees up time for the analysis that actually matters.

Which step in your workflow is overpaying for a model?
carousel: Slide 1: $30 to analyze 15,000 accounts of sales calls.
Slide 2: Stop using your smartest model for every step.
Slide 3: Classification is repetitive. A lower-level model like Claude Haiku can handle it.
Slide 4: Bold? Try DeepSeek on a Fireworks API to cut costs further.
Slide 5: Cheap classification lets you analyze a team's entire call history.
Slide 6: Track MEDDIC averages, then chart each rep's improvement over time.
Slide 7: Compare regrettable versus non-regrettable attrition. Does MEDDIC growth track performance?
Slide 8: Stop stopping at surface-level reporting. Ask the deeper questions.

lesson.title: Match the model to the step
takeaways: Classification steps don't need your most powerful model. A lower-level model like Claude Haiku can do the job.
Cheaper models dramatically cut costs. The estimate for 15,000 accounts of one sales team's history was $30.
Low cost frees you to ask second, third, and fourth order questions beyond surface-level reporting.
lesson.exercise: List every step in one AI workflow you run. Mark the ones that are pure classification, then rerun those on a lower-level model and compare cost and output quality.

caption: $30 for 15,000 accounts

A week of analysis now takes hours.

The analyses I spin up for leadership used to take me about a week to put together. Now they take a couple of hours.
